The research community today faces a serious challenge: the underlying purpose of science has shifted. Scientists ought to serve science itself, driven by the joy of investigation, discovery, and new findings. Unfortunately, many researchers now pursue science primarily for reputation and career advancement, turning the enterprise into a business‑like endeavor. 

My own predoctoral project was recently accepted by *Nature Communications*. While colleagues celebrated the publication as a stepping stone to higher earnings and a distinguished career—recognizing the importance of impact factors—I feel a different sense of pride. I am grateful for the achievement, yet I wish the most valued aspect of my work were the results themselves, the science I have contributed.

Q26.text: I studied for over 8 years to be where I am now. I do not have student debt. I was a straight As student in school and in college. But regardless I turned out to be a shit scientist -- no publications (inc. in sight), no conferences attended even with a poster, I am not sure whether my research will yield something presentable. I cannot network or promote myself. I do not write well. If I graduate without a paper, I am looking at a mediocre lab postdoc position at best with median year salary ~$45k. I do not know how I will afford rent, savings for the future, taking care of my parents -- I am the only child. I do not know whether I can land an industry job in the competitive environment over-producing PhDs.  I heard about people who get scholarships and earn 30-50% above the typical postdoc salary. They apply for grants and quickly become PIs to earn their lower three figures. Or they aim for green cards through H1B or EB2, paying for the mistake of being born in a shit third-world country, through living off $45k for several years to then end a better paying job in industry. Both options require publishing at least three first author papers, having citations, getting funding, networking -- all the things I don't see myself doing as of now. There are labs that are more collaborative and people end up helping with other peoples' projects and with more papers in the end. I am not in one of them. People who chose different majors -- programming or medicine -- can get bioinformatician or clinical fellow salaries doing same science next to me but earning two times more. Their salaries approaching market because they have a choice. I do not have a choice. Why did no one stop me at any point? How did I end up here? What am I going to do in the future? I think academic system feeds on people like me luring us with promises of meaningful job and hard work paying off and shits us out. It is not healthy to work weekends. It is not healthy to sometimes go months without seeing any progress. It is not healthy to over-sell results in publications just to survive in this environment.

Q26.text: I think there is overall, a focus on all the wrong things in getting a PhD. People get PhDs for different reasons, but the system is setup only for those who want to pursue careers in academia. To get a career in academia, you throw out most of what it means to push the boundaries of knowledge. Instead, you focus on paper count, no matter how incremental or banal the contribution of each paper is. There's too much focus on image and research fads, and not enough stoking of creativity and exploration. I've been told many times to not go down an interesting (to me) path because my advisor/peers could not predict where it would go, or whether it would be successful and get funding. Isn't that the whole point of trying to expand knowledge? To pursue something simply because you don't know where it will go and what will become of it. Instead, we focus on the low hanging fruit that will get the most papers and attract the most attention.

Q55.text: You can have many great ideas, but they are often dismissed as too risky or not aligned with others’ interests. As a PhD student you occupy a low rung on the academic hierarchy, so unless you have independent funding, your advisor will typically steer you toward projects that advance their own work. If you are determined to earn a doctorate, you must be prepared to navigate countless hoops. You can react with frustration and burnout—something I have seen happen to many students—or you can accept the reality, keep in mind that you will eventually have more control over your own path, and push through the obstacles until you reach your goal. I don’t endorse the current system, but this is how it works for most doctoral programs today.
Q55.original_text: You can have lots of good ideas that people will say no to because it is too risky, or doesn't align with their own interests. As a PhD student you are pretty low on the totem pole, so unless you are independently funded, your advisor will ask you to do things that promote their own work. If you are determined to get a PhD, then you have to be resigned to jumping through countless hoops, and you can choose to be angry about it and just be miserable (as I've seen many students burn out on), or you can accept it, remember that in the future you will be more in charge of your path, and jump through the hoops until you get there. It doesn't mean I agree with the way things are, but to get through a doctorate program, that's how it currently is.

Q41.text:
I would most like to work as a researcher at a national laboratory such as NASA, or at a non‑profit research institute. I haven’t ruled out staying in academia entirely, but I’ve found that entry‑level faculty positions (assistant professor and the like) no longer align with my research goals or with the expectations I had before pursuing an advanced degree. Academic departments tend to prioritize projects that are “known” to succeed; funding is typically awarded only to low‑risk proposals, leaving well‑conceived but high‑risk ideas on the shelf.

I’m not certain that non‑academic research institutes operate differently, and I’m not fully versed in their structures and expectations. Nonetheless, I feel that traditional academia is not the right fit for me at this point. While some universities—and especially senior scholars who have already established themselves—might share my view of knowledge pursuit, I want to explore a new environment for the foreseeable future.

Ideally I would love to become an astronaut, but that prospect is extremely unlikely. Instead, I’m eager to work with motivated, intelligent collaborators who are willing to push the boundaries of knowledge driven by pure curiosity.
Q41.original_text: I would most like to work as a researcher in a national lab (like NASA) or a non-profit research institute. I have not dismissed the idea completely in continuing in academia, but I have seen how, at least on the lower level (assistant professor, etc), the goals of pursuing research do not align with mine, or what I believed of academia before pursuing an advanced degree. There is too much focus on pursuing ideas that are "known" to succeed. Funding is only handed out to those projects that are likely to succeed, leaving out the well explained/though out ideas that have a high chance of failure. I don't really think non-academic research institutes are any different. I am not well versed in the structure and expectations of non-academic research institutes, but I know that academia isn't quite the right fit. Other universities, and certainly for those academics who have already proven themselves, might adhere more to my thoughts on the pursuit of knowledge, but for the foreseeable future I want to try somewhere new.  Ideally, I'd like to be an astronaut, but as that is extremely unlikely, I'm interested in getting to pursue ideas with other motivated, intelligent collaborators that push the boundaries of knowledge for the sake of curiosity.

Q60.text:
The feedback loop between researchers and prospective funders is gradually shutting down promising lines of inquiry. Too often, decisions are driven by fleeting trends and by individuals—such as politicians—who lack the expertise to shape the future of research.

Working in a relatively new discipline, I have watched the foundations of the field being laid and have seen newly appointed professors launch their laboratories. What I observe is that these foundations are frequently flashy but fragile. They prioritize projects that will capture public attention, neglecting the underlying science. When the craze subsides, the “flash” offers nothing to sustain the effort, and the entire structure collapses.

Because funding and positions are increasingly tied to eye‑catching demonstrations rather than substantive work, researchers feel compelled to produce superficial spectacles to survive. I worry that this pattern will worsen as anti‑intellectual sentiment grows and more like‑minded individuals are placed in positions of power. The result is a vicious cycle that threatens to implode unless a critical mass of people unite to protect the pursuit of knowledge for its own sake.

This is far from the ideal of academia I once imagined; my experience has revealed how petty and short‑sighted the system can be.
Q60.original_text: The feedback loop between researchers and potential funding agencies is slowly closing off potentially fruitful research avenues because of fads that are relying too heavily on people who are not qualified to determine the future of research (e.g. politicians). I am in a relatively young field so I've had the opportunity to watch the foundations get built, and see newly anointed professors start their labs. From what I've seen, the foundations are flashy and weak. They focus on what will capture the public's attention without regards to the fundamental science, and at some point the foundation will collapse because the fad will fade and the flash has nothing to fall back on when extinguished. However, no jobs (or funding) is available unless you can blind those in charge with a flashy demo that has no real substance. I fear this is a general trend that will only get worse as the population of those who abhor intelligence and curiosity grows and continue to appoint like minded individuals to positions of power. It is a vicious cycle that is heading for collapse, unless enough people can band together to preserve the pursuit of knowledge for the sake of knowledge This was what I thought academia was, until I was embedded in the midst of it, and saw how very petty academia can be.

Q26.text: Sadly, the only important criteria for success in academia is the amount of published material. This often leads to rivals among senior and junior researchers, where the former is more likely to get the credit even for work performed by the junior person (e.g. author list on publications). A race for publishing is so intense since most staff contracts (PhD stipends) depend on the amount and impact of publications within a certain time frame (e.g. 3 years for a PhD in life sciences).      Unfortunately, moral standards at some German institutions are at its lowest level: A new research institute that is yet to receive its academic recognition will rather ignore repeated complaints on staff injustice and academic misconduct than risk a bad reputation. Likewise, a young PI will refuse to protect and stand behind a victim of sabotage and pretend all is fine, as long as there is a possibility for a new publication from the person doing the injustice.       PhD students are often subjected to exploitation with no protection since at the end of the day everyone needs that critical reference letter to pursue the next step in an academic career.

Q26.text: In many ways, the current system feels archaic and resistant to change. Principal investigators (PIs) should have only limited influence over a student’s academic trajectory. We tend to assume that PIs provide appropriate mentorship and training, yet few actually consider these responsibilities in depth or develop a clear approach to them. Many PIs simply react to situations as they arise; while not inherently wrong, this reactive stance often fails to offer proactive support. Graduate‑program administrators should therefore establish detailed criteria and milestones, hold PIs accountable to them, and, if necessary, reassign students to other mentors without jeopardizing the students’ time to graduation.
Q26.original_text: In many ways it feels like systems are extremely archaic and resistant to change. For example, PIs should have very little power over their students academic trajectory: we assume that they are providing appropriate mentorship and training, but in very few situations have PIs explicitly thought about these things and figured out how to approach them. Many PIs seem to just do what comes to them in the moment, which isn't necessarily wrong, but also isn't often proactively helpful. Rather, I think graduate program administrators should be setting out detailed criteria and milestones and holding PIs accountable to those, perhaps even by reassigning  students to other PIs without penalty to the student's graduation time.

Q26.text: As a PhD student I have to collect a certain amount of points in order to be able to complete a PhD study program. Those points can be obtained from a variety of activities like attending conferences/meetings, courses (both directly related to the thesis topic or focusing on soft skills development) or having papers published. Only students who complete the study program can submit their thesis. University requirement for the thesis is to have at least one paper accepted, however there is an unwritten rule in my lab that students need to have at least 2 accepted papers one submitted and one ready to be send. The submitted thesis (approved by supervisor)  is being revised by internal committee (experts in the field from the University) and once approved is being send to the external committee members (experts in the field from outside the University). Only when the thesis is approved by the external committee members the public defense can take place. So obtaining a PhD degree at the University I am currently studding is a complex and multitask challenge.

Q26.text:
My experience has been a mix of both positive and negative elements, largely shaped by the supervisors I worked with and the support I received from my doctoral school.

I began my PhD under a supervisor who proved to be manipulative, indecisive, and outright bullying. The “great science” touted in the lab turned out to be poorly substantiated work with tiny sample sizes. Fortunately, the staff at the doctoral school recognized the problem and helped me find a new supervisor and a new project.

My second supervisor was a genuinely kind person. Working with him allowed me to regain a normal mental state, and he gave me the freedom to lead my own project. He wasn’t perfect in every respect, but I learned how to collaborate with him, and over time we built a strong, respectful relationship. This taught me the importance of recognizing a colleague’s limits and investing the right amount of effort to obtain guidance or leadership when needed.

The system itself is not fundamentally flawed; rather, it is the individuals within it who can make a difference. My determination to earn my PhD never waned, even after the first supervisor left me feeling depressed, sleep‑deprived, and, at age 28, occasionally bedwetting. Those difficulties nearly destroyed a personal relationship, which I am still working to repair.

The turning point came when an advisor from the doctoral program began checking in with me after our weekly seminars—often over a beer in the classroom. When I finally opened up, I broke down in tears, and those conversations became the foundation for the help I needed. The advisor listened without dismissing my concerns, helped me understand what was wrong, and guided me toward solutions that protected my mental health. Their support was not a predetermined pathway; instead, they empowered me to make informed decisions and treated my struggles seriously.

From this experience I can say that PhD programs need dedicated advisors—separate from research supervisors—who can build trust and genuinely care for students. My program has had such a position for several years, and evaluations show it outperforms other French doctoral programs (the former FdV, now FIRE). I believe this success stems from the advisors’ commitment to students’ well‑being.

Throughout the four‑year program we also attended numerous “soft‑skills” workshops. These sessions highlighted career opportunities beyond academia, taught work‑life balance, and offered guidance on self‑presentation. They were instrumental in keeping me afloat. I have heard many stories of students who lacked this support network and whose PhDs ended poorly because they felt isolated and unheard.

In France, the academic system distinguishes between the laboratory (where the research is done) and the graduate school (often housed in a separate building). Having a common space where we could meet, interact, and build community proved invaluable. Competent advisors and peers provided constructive advice—not merely a venue for venting—ensuring we remained scientifically rigorous while also protecting our mental health. Whether that meant scaling back ambitions, taking a leave, or even leaving the PhD entirely, the final decision always rested with the student, whose needs must be respected without compromising high scientific standards.

Q60.text: Thanks for performing this survey. This is an extremely important topic that is often overlooked. We are looked at as cheap labor (and often young) labor that needs to pay their dues. But often it comes at the cost of our mental and physical health. My mental and physical health has significantly declined over the past 4 years that I've been in my PhD program. I've definitely experienced depression and anxiety, and have had many more visits to the doctor for physical health problems. A back problem from sitting for 12 hours a day at the computer, problems with my hands from typing so much, other problems from increasing my drinking (to cope with stress), a urinary tract infection from holding my urine too long because I don't have time to pee because I am working; I've often put off medical appointments due to lack of time as well. Students often put off their health like they are in survival mode and tell themselves "it's okay to not be healthy for a while" because when you are done with the program you will have time to be healthy. But after years of putting off your health and happiness, living in "survival mode" becomes unbearable. That combined with feeling like you have no control over your own labor nor are getting compensated a livable wage for it can be extremely depressing. Granted some students are predisposed to having more health problems than others as a result of the stressors of a PhD program--however, there are major problems with the system and culture of PhD education that need to be fixed to support student health.

Q26.text: De ce que je peux observer, les professeurs semblent avoir une grosse charge de travail (demandes de subvention, préparation des cours, travail administratif, tâches départementales, etc.) ce qui fait qu'ils ont peu de temps à consacrer à la recherche et aux travaux que leurs étudiants aux cycles supérieurs font. De plus, il semble y avoir une certaine « game politique » afin d'optimiser ses chances d'obtenir des subventions. Ainsi, dès lors qu'un professeur respecte ses valeurs fondamentales qui l'empêchent de jouer cette « game politique », il devient très difficile pour lui de faire rouler efficacement son laboratoire, ce qui est notre cas. Au cours des années, faute de financement, nous avons perdu des techniciens et des associés de recherche pour nous aider dans nos travaux, diminuant ainsi notre capacité à produire des publications de qualité. Or, le système actuel semble juger la valeur d'un groupe de recherche presque exclusivement sur le nombre de publications que ce dernier produit (et pas nécessairement sur le nombre de publications de qualité), ce qui nous fait entrer dans un cercle vicieux dont il est presque impossible de sortir. Ayant choisi mes études supérieures en fonction de mes intérêts et non du succès du groupe de recherche, mes possibilités de publication tôt dans mes études ont été inexistantes, m'empêchant par le fait même d'avoir accès à la majorité des bourses d'études qui évaluent le potentiel de recherche d'un candidat en fonction de son nombre de publications. Avoir su cela plus tôt, j'aurais dû faire une maîtrise dans un gros groupe de recherche connaissant du succès afin que mon nom apparaisse sur plusieurs publications. Une chance que mon université m'aide financièrement, car sinon je n'aurais jamais pu faire la recherche que je fais actuellement.

Q26.text: O sistema acadêmico da república tcheca é bastante focado em produção.  Não se importa muito a defesa de uma tese, da ideia em si.  Apenas vejo que o programas de PhD em geral esqueceram da onde vem a sigla Ph.D e não discutem mais as coisas no âmbito argumentativo.  Não importam tanto com o racional do projeto, com a hipótese do projeto... e a defesa argumentativa que deveria ser feita.  Maioria dos projetos vejo que começa simplesmente por que temos dinheiro e estrutura. Mas não porque temos um grande racional e uma justificativa para tentar lançar uma hipótese a ser defendida por provas a posteriori.    Na minha concepção,  Tudo deveria iniciar com uma ideia sólida.  Uma hipótese a qual todos não consigam derrubar com argumentos. Sendo interessante alocar recursos escassos para responder uma pergunta da qual necessita-se de uma resposta a posteriori.    O sistema então acaba valorizando bastante dados soltos, contudo ainda sim são resultados. E acaba desvalorizando o tempo 'perdido' no campo das ideias.   A quantidade muitas vezes parece ser mais importante do que a qualidade . Infelizmente vejo que o sistema recompensa este tipo de mentalidade.  No Brasil (país onde fiz meu mestrado), não era diferente.   Com isso , o sistema que criamos é um sistema preocupado com técnicos. Pessoas que vangloriam por saber determinada técnica.  Pois em teoria, isto traz mais produção.  As pessoas não entendem que aprender técnica é apenas uma questão de tempo e prática. Não precisa de raciocínio lógico. Sendo que em muitos institutos grandes, você de fato tem técnicos e facilities para fazer o trabalho técnico para você.   No entanto, técnica pode ser aplicada mil vezes... mas se não estiver denfendendo uma ideia não fará nenhum sentido fazer por fazer.   Acredito que precisamos fazer um esforço para mudar esta mentalidade nos institutos ao redor do mundo.  A revista Nature é muito conceituada e acredito que ela representa bem a amostragem dos institutos que de fato estão preocupados em mover o mundo através de ideias.    Pedro Zeni
